title: Is it this you'd miss?
hookLine: afraid of death? is it this particular errand you'd miss? (Meditations 10.29)
tomorrow: Let no one say it truly

cards: You're refolding towels. Answering the fourteenth email about the same meeting. Scrolling past a video you've already seen three times.
Then someone leans in and asks: if you had to leave this life today, is this what you'd miss? It's an odd question over a basket of laundry, and an odd one to ask yourself at all.
But Marcus asks it in book ten of the Meditations, and he asks it of everything he does.

teach.h: STOP AND ASK, IN EVERY ACT.
teach.b: In every single thing you do, Marcus writes, stop and ask yourself: is death terrible because it takes this away from me? That's the whole entry.
He's pointing the question at his own fear of dying. Much of what fills an hour isn't something we'd miss.
If death is frightening because it would take away this errand, this complaint, this scroll, then the fear is smaller than it seemed. But the question cuts the other way too.
If you look at what you're doing and the honest answer is, no, I wouldn't miss this, then why does so much of the day go to it?

The question that loosens the fear of death also sorts the hours of a life. Some things pass the test easily: a long talk at the kitchen table, the evening walk, the work that matters to you. And this isn't contempt.
Marcus isn't saying ordinary life is worthless. A few entries earlier, he told himself to be content with what is given now. Towels still need folding.
The point isn't to despise the errand.
It's to see it at its real size, so it doesn't carry more weight than it should, in your fears or in your hours.
And Marcus leaves it as he found it: a question, asked again in every act.

how: Some readers of the Meditations pause during routine tasks and ask Marcus's question, which helps them see trivial worries at their real size and notice which parts of the day they truly value.

practice: Pick one ordinary task from today, something done or still waiting, and ask Marcus's question honestly: is this what I'd miss? If the answer is no, notice what that does to the task; maybe it gets lighter, or shorter.
If it's yes, notice that too, and let it be precious.
